name: Agent: Video Production
summary: Turns a brief into finished social video — the footage, the edit, the music, the voice-over, the captions — with a person approving before anything costs money.
objectives: Finished video straight from Claude: footage, edit, music, voice-over, captions and quality checks in one run.
The best quality for the lowest cost.
Ten to thirty social videos per campaign, as themed versions of one main video.
Add a new brand by adding a folder. The agent itself never changes.
Nothing that costs money runs until a person says go.

outcomes.text: It made a full campaign: one main video and three themed versions, each in two languages and three shapes, with captions burned in and a subtitle file per language. A person approved every step.

The cheap check caught the expensive mistake. A generated image came back with broken English written on it — in an ad for an English school. It was thrown out at the sketch stage, for the price of a picture instead of the price of a finished video.

Every cost is checked before it is spent, recorded job by job, and matched afterwards against the provider's own receipt. A cost the provider never reports gets marked as missing, instead of quietly counted as zero.

Using it for real found four faults in the agent itself — music that never actually got mixed in, a version that inherited the wrong voice-over. Each one became a fix, plus a test that fails if it ever comes back.
The quality check now checks itself. It used to report all-clear while running one of the four checks it promised. The videos were fine; the all-clear was not worth much until this was fixed.

One thing it has not done yet: generate its own footage. The campaign it made end to end used client material that was already shot and silent, so the AI generation, the two languages and the native-speaker review have never all run on one real job.

That run is the next step and it is deliberately gated: a real brief, a person's go-ahead, and a ceiling of 100 credits. Until it happens, the agent is proven as a pipeline and unproven as a producer.

Every price it quotes was checked against the real account, and three were wrong. A quote is a floor, not a forecast: one job quoted at 22 credits cost 90. And a plan feature called "unlimited" is real only in a browser — the agent uses another door, where it still pays.

The music rule was strict in a way that made no sense: it refused a properly licensed track for the sole reason that a machine made it. The test is now the licence, confirmed by a person. What did not change is the part that bites: no recorded licence, no music — the video ships silent and says why.

Dubbing into another language was costed from a guess of about 100 credits. The two real jobs on record cost 121 and 142 — so one language alone would eat a third of the budget set aside for an entire test campaign. It is written down as priced and not yet available, rather than quietly offered.

The model list can now be refreshed by a command that shows what changed and waits for approval. It edits single lines instead of rewriting the file, because most of that file explains why each price is what it is — and it stops rather than guess when a model appears or disappears.

The intake form was rebuilt around how a campaign is actually run, not just where it gets published. One question — "which channel?" — turned out to be three: what kind of video, how it gets made, and where it ships. Nine parts of the system depend on the third meaning, so it kept its name.

The form now offers things the agent cannot yet do — TV ads, two editing tools, brand characters — and marks each one instead of hiding it. The request gets recorded; the run gets blocked. Asking for something we cannot build yet is useful information, not a mistake to reject.

It will not render a language nobody agreed to review. Open English ships to four markets and two are Spanish — Latin America and Spain are different copy read by different people, so they count as two. Spain and Turkey have no reviewer yet, so both are blocked.

Review texts can now be sent to the reviewer by Slack, a shared document, or email. Sending is not approving: the video stays blocked until that person's sign-off is actually written down, for every language separately.
Every finished file now lands in one folder named after the ticket that asked for it, so a delivery can be traced back to its request without anyone remembering a naming rule.

The form used to carry one brand's settings inside the shared agent, which meant adding a brand required editing the tool. Those settings moved out to the brand's own folder, and the shared form now refuses to open without one rather than showing an empty page that looks like it works.

Text now sits where the platform leaves room for it, by construction rather than by eye. Every caption, logo and on-screen line is placed from one written-down set of margins — so the layout and the check that grades it cannot disagree.

Three of the six layouts could not be described the old way at all. YouTube's top edge is a staircase, not a straight line, and flattening it would have thrown away about a fifth of the usable width of every wide video.
The social layout has a column of buttons covering only the lower half of the screen. Treating that as a permanent margin would have surrendered space that is free everywhere above it.

The quality gate used to answer a smaller question than people read into it: it confirmed a layout existed for the target platform, never that anything was inside it. Those are now two checks, and the second fails a batch when a caption or logo strays.

Square and portrait-crop layouts have no official reference yet, so they are marked provisional and every review still is stamped PROVISIONAL. A guess and a measurement should never look the same to whoever approves the work.

A video cut for one shape is not automatically safe in another — the square version crops the top off the tall one. Positions are now worked out against every shape a campaign ships, and checked again separately for each.

The tool that keeps platform specs current can no longer overwrite the official layouts; it proposes and stops. As it was, one approved refresh would have deleted forty lines explaining why those numbers are what they are.

Eleven safeguards were each deliberately broken on a scrap copy to confirm the tests catch them. Eleven for eleven — and the harness refuses to count a crashed test as a test that caught something, which is how its own first run turned out to be false alarms.

The brief form now works from a link, so anyone can fill one in without a copy of the repo. It ships empty: you load your own project's settings in your browser, and they never leave your machine. The page has no way to send them anywhere, and the browser is what enforces that.

Getting it ready to publish found the form was quietly carrying things that belong to us: what two real jobs cost on our account, two supplier names, an internal chat channel, a real ticket number. Not secret exactly — and all of it would have been on a public page.

So there is now a check that reads the projects folder and refuses to publish if anything from it — a client name, a person's name, a shared link, a brand colour — has been typed into the shared form. Add a client and the check covers them without anyone remembering.
That check caught its own author twice: once flagging a comment written while explaining the rule, and once, after being committed, flagging itself.

The form was rebuilt around what a choice will cost. A list down the side shows what still has to be fixed and, separately, what will stop the video being made — because asking for something we cannot build yet is worth recording, not rejecting.

All thirty option buttons were unreachable by keyboard and invisible to a screen reader, and no field had a proper label. Both fixed. Colours are now measured for whatever brand is loaded, which found a selected option whose label had always been below the legibility line.

The narrow-screen check had been passing on a picture rather than a layout: the preview tool cannot go below a certain width, so a phone-sized screenshot was really a crop of a desktop one. Measured properly, the page ran 473 pixels off the side of a phone. It does not now.
El formulario ya está publicado y funcionando: https://oegit.github.io/oe-campaign-intake/ — cualquiera del equipo lo abre sin tener una copia del repositorio.

Se comprobó contra la página servida, no contra la intención: lo que entrega la dirección es byte por byte el archivo revisado, sale vacío como debe, y un intento de mandar datos afuera lo bloquea el navegador.
Antes se compartía otro archivo distinto, que sólo funcionaba dentro del chat de Claude y hoy está dos días desactualizado. Esa vía nunca sirvió para la versión publicable; el enlace la reemplaza.

milestones.title: Write the agent: what it makes, in what order, and where a person decides
Keep every model choice in one file, so switching models is not a code change
Build the edit template and the export formats
Make cost something you check before spending, not after
Prove the whole pipeline on a throwaway brand, spending nothing
Debug it on a real run and fix what that broke
Add the voice-over and the captions, in every language
Make a real campaign end to end and get it approved
Turn the quality check's own blind spots into tests
Check every price against the real account and correct what was wrong
Rebuild the intake form around how a campaign is actually run, not just where it is published
Put the official safe-zone layouts to work — text placed from them, and a check that fails when it strays
